learning_outcomes.text: Understand the basic principles and concepts of using modern spectroscopic techniques in the field of materials science, such as UV-vis spectroscopy, Infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), Raman spectroscopy, X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (XRF), nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR).
Obtain basic experience of how important spectroscopic techniques are to materials science.
Searching, analysis and synthesis of data and information, with the use of the necessary technology.

syllabus_topics: Beer-Lambert Law, Electronic transitions, Visible range of the spectrum, Color - wavelength relation, Typical examples of chemical compound spectra, Absorption/Transmission/Reflection spectra in liquid and solid samples.

Dipolar moment, Vibrational/Rotational energy levels, Types of molecular vibrational motion, Selection rules, Instrumentation, Michelson Interferometer, Typical FT-IR spectra of organic compounds, Attenuated Total Reflectance (ATR), Applications.

Basic principles, Stokes/Anti-Stokes lines, Polarization, Vibration - Rotation types, Selection rules, Comparison with FT-IR: similarities and differences, laser, Instrumentation, Typical Raman spectra of organic and inorganic compounds / materials, Applications.

Basic principles, electronic transitions (ground and excited states), Selection rules, Instrumentation (fluorimeter), Typical fluorescence spectra of compounds, Laser Induced Fluorescence (LIF), Applications.

Magnetic field, spin, fission, Principle of chemical shift, Spectrum Types (Hydrogen 1H and Carbon 13C), Single and Multidimensional spectra (COSY, HMQC, etc.), Instrumentation, Applications in organic compounds.
teaching_methods: Homework and creation - presentation of specific slides
Finding of time and space in laboratories for demo experiments in correlation to the theory

assessment_methods.method: Preparation and presentation of a topic related to spectroscopy (in groups)
Final written examination (multiple-choice questions and developing of topics)

assessment_rules: Students are evaluated by their presence and participation in the lectures, by questions and exercises during the lectures, and by the preparation and presentation of a topic related to spectroscopy (in groups). Students are also evaluated by a final written examination in Greek that includes a combination of multiple-choice questions and developing of topics.
